FLIGHT STUDY

Preparing embedded geometry, material response and technical views.

01 / Concept engineering brief

A new ground plane.
A different way to move.

Super Motor explores a compact, enclosed hover vehicle built around a faceted hull and prominent lateral rotor housings. This interactive study connects the supplied animated geometry to an explicitly proposed mission, propulsion architecture and development programme.

VERTASCAN / CONCEPTSBYDANOCTOBER 2026
850kg / mass target
360kW / installed target
80kWh / energy target

Proposal status. The source GLB proves visual form and animation only. Dimensions in metres, mass, power, range, control authority and mission performance below are study assumptions, not measured capabilities, manufacturing specifications or an airworthiness claim.

01 / What the source establishes

The visible design combines an angular enclosed body, large circular side structures, a low perimeter frame and a strongly articulated mechanical silhouette. The surface language alternates light panel fields, dark mechanical zones, glass-like materials and emissive details. Its protected cabin and broad rotor housings suggest a short-range utility vehicle, while the height and mechanical massing make it less suited to a conventional road-car package.

The asset has five mesh records, sixteen material definitions, three embedded JPEG textures and four rotation clips approximately 4.15 seconds long. The active scene includes the hull, cylinder and two rotor nodes. A seat-cushion mesh exists outside the active hierarchy; this presentation preserves the active source scene rather than adding unplaced geometry. The animation mixer plays the source propulsion clips at idle and increases their playback speed under flight demand. Hull rotation is available separately for design review so it does not overwrite navigation.

Existing UV coordinates and the source vent texture transform remain intact. Surface treatment adjusts anisotropic filtering, colour space, metal reflectance, matte hull roughness, glass opacity and emissive output. It does not create new UV islands or claim to recover missing detail. Terrain uses a view-dependent height-map relief shader, bump response and procedural diffuse maps; the vehicle keeps its original texture layout.

02 / Design intent and mission

The proposed role is a piloted site-to-site mobility platform for controlled industrial campuses, research ranges and infrastructure surveys. Its useful advantage would be crossing interrupted ground without a road surface: pale desert flats, wet forest clearings and prepared urban service corridors. The first deployment case is a surveyed, fenced test route with a staffed hangar, no public overflight and designated landing areas.

In a desert survey mission, the vehicle transports a pilot and compact sensor payload between instrument stations, maintaining a low hover for local positioning and transitioning to forward motion across open terrain. For a jungle inspection, the realistic route follows an established clearing rather than weaving through dense canopy. In a city demonstration, the scenario is a closed district or prepared landing deck; the illuminated street canyon here tests camera visibility and interaction, not permission to operate in an urban airspace.

The parked hangar state is also part of the use case: maintenance crews need access around the housings, a defined rotor exclusion zone, visible readiness indications and an unobstructed departure path. The procedural hangar provides structure, lighting strips, storage props, floor guidance and a powered doorway. The flight demo raises the vehicle before moving through the opening, then hands control to the user.

04 / Lift, energy and feasibility

At 850 kg, static weight is approximately 8.34 kN. Two assumed 2.2 m disks give a combined ideal disk area of 7.60 m² and a disk loading of about 1.10 kN/m². Using sea-level air density of 1.225 kg/m³, ideal momentum-theory hover power P = T³ᐟ² / √(2ρA) is approximately 176 kW. A notional overall lift-system efficiency of 55% increases electrical hover demand to roughly 320 kW, before allowing for auxiliaries; this study budgets about 330 kW.

This is the principal feasibility constraint. An 80 kWh pack with 64 kWh usable supports only about 11.6 minutes at 330 kW. A 30-minute mission would require a substantial reduction in forward-flight power: four minutes of combined take-off/landing hover consume about 22 kWh, while twenty-six minutes at an assumed 90 kW consume 39 kWh. The resulting 61 kWh leaves only 3 kWh inside the usable budget. That margin is too small for wind, degraded cells, routing delays or hot-day lift losses; the first operational target should be shorter until measurement justifies expansion.

The visible rotor structures do not establish effective lift area or thrust direction. A viable vehicle needs verified lift-vector geometry, anti-torque behaviour, pitch and roll authority, and an acceptable centre of gravity. Two motor units alone do not demonstrate controllability after one fails. Independent controllers, protected buses and a flight computer improve fault containment, but a safe loss-of-thrust strategy remains an open engineering requirement.

05 / Engineering capabilities to develop

Propulsion and cooling. Motor/inverter packages would be integrated near the housings with short high-current paths, monitored bearings and contained rotating elements. At 330 kW electrical input, even a 92% motor/inverter efficiency produces roughly 26 kW of heat in those components, before battery and other losses. Liquid cooling, controlled radiator airflow and temperature-limited torque therefore belong in the primary architecture, not a later cosmetic addition.

Flight control. The proposal uses inertial sensors, satellite positioning, lidar or radar altitude, and a supervised state machine for idle, lift, translation, approach and landing. Thrust vectoring or variable pitch must produce commanded moments around all three axes. Low-speed damping and pilot override would be tested with a tethered rig before unrestricted flight. In this HTML, acceleration, yaw, climb, banking and contact are intentionally simplified demonstration behaviour; telemetry is generated by the demo.

Structure and protection. The perimeter frame could carry landing loads and protect the lower body, but mesh thickness is not a structural section. Rotor-ring stiffness, mounting fatigue, crash load paths, battery retention and cabin protection need analysis from a reconstructed engineering CAD model. Composite skins could reduce fairing mass, while metallic hard points carry propulsion loads. Maintainable access panels and clear component separation would be necessary before an assembly plan.

Environment and human factors. Desert dust creates ingestion and abrasion risks; wet vegetation raises debris and electrical protection concerns; city façades create recirculation and gusts. Ground wash and noise may dominate site selection. The demonstration's idle bass, hover harmonics and thrust noise are synthesised design cues, not an acoustic prediction. Likewise, atmospheric haze and luminous cones are visual presentation effects rather than computational fluid dynamics.

06 / Development and verification

01
Geometry & packaging audit

Resolve source scale, rotor axes, cabin occupancy, centre-of-gravity range, real lift area, clearances and access. Reconstruct thicknesses and interfaces in engineering CAD.

02
Propulsion bench & energy tests

Measure thrust versus input power, duct pressure loss, motor heat, vibration and pack voltage sag. Replace assumed efficiency with a measured operating map.

03
Structural and tethered validation

Test mounting loads, rotor containment, landing interfaces and restraint systems. Verify control moments, sensor failure handling and loss-of-power response on a tether.

04
Controlled flight envelope

Start with short low-hover sorties at a closed range, then expand speed and duration using logged energy, temperature, handling and noise data. Public operation requires a separate certification and operational process.

07 / What the interactive scene demonstrates

The presentation embeds the original GLB and source animation clips in one offline HTML. Six parallel-projection views document the active geometry without perspective distortion. Three seeded environments support repeatable visual review, while the service hangar offers a lit idle scene, auto departure and return/reset. Manual movement includes acceleration, reverse, yaw, climb, descent, boost, braking and simplified obstacle contact. Spatially positioned tonal audio follows camera-to-craft distance; thrust noise follows movement demand. These features support a design conversation; they do not certify flight physics.
